input.rationale: Seventy-second pass: close the eligibility side of the witness work with a safety check. Earlier passes established that witnesses count as voting members for quorum, read confirmation and commit, which raises the natural question of whether a witness or observer can also campaign and lead a cluster that it never replicates. Reading the tick path and the state transitions settles it: the non-leader tick returns before the election check for observers and witnesses, the transition into candidate state refuses both roles, and the election request itself is skipped while a membership change is committed but not yet applied. This pass records the exclusion and an explained negative.

investigations.question: Can a witness or observer node campaign for leadership, and does anything stop a node from starting an election while a membership change is committed but not yet applied?
investigations.hypothesis: The non-leader tick returns before the election check for observers and witnesses, the transition into candidate state refuses both roles, and an election request is skipped while a membership change is committed but not applied, so neither role can lead and the config-change window cannot produce a leader with a stale view of the quorum.

knowledge.statement: On every non-leader tick the election counter advances and rate-limit work may run, but the election check is skipped when the node is an observer or a witness, so neither role ever proposes itself as a candidate. The transition into candidate state independently refuses both roles and panics if it is reached, which makes the exclusion a structural invariant rather than a single check. A separate guard covers the configuration-change window: an election request is ignored while a membership change is committed but not applied, because a node with a stale view of the membership could otherwise win with a quorum that does not overlap the quorum that committed the change.
knowledge.conditions: A node is in observer or witness state and its election timer would otherwise expire, or any non-leader node receives an election request while a membership change is committed but not yet applied.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a witness or observer cannot campaign, so the earlier finding that both roles count toward quorum does not extend to leadership, and the commit and read-confirmation duties they carry are the only leadership-adjacent duties they have. The tick path shows the exclusion: a non-leader tick advances the election counter and may run rate-limit work, then returns before the election check when the node is an observer or a witness, citing section 4.2.1 of the thesis (raft.go:574-597). The state transition enforces the same rule independently: becomeCandidate refuses leader, observer and witness states, panicking for the latter two, so no other path can quietly turn a witness into a candidate (raft.go:971-983). A third guard covers a different hazard on the same axis: an election request is ignored while a membership change is committed but not applied, with a comment working through a three-node example where a node with a stale membership could win with a quorum that does not overlap the quorum that committed the change (raft.go:1511-1526). Together these make the voter-eligibility account consistent: witnesses and observers contribute to the quorum arithmetic that already commits and confirms, but they cannot lead. Two bounds belong with the account: this trace covers campaigning, not voting, so whether a witness grants votes in an election is a separate path that this pass did not read, and the config-change guard is described only by its own comment and condition, without an executed scenario.

knowledge.assertion: Observers and witnesses never pass the election check, and candidate transitions refuse both roles.

counterevidence: Witnesses and observers still count toward the quorum that elects a leader, so their support can decide an election even though they cannot stand in one.
The config-change guard depends on the node knowing that a change is committed but not applied; a node whose applied index already covers the change proceeds normally.
limitations: Source trace only: no election was executed for this question.
The vote-granting path for witnesses and observers was not traced, so this account covers campaigning only.
The config-change election guard is read from its condition and comment, without an executed example of the stale-quorum hazard it describes.

knowledge.statement: Every raft state transition (becomeFollower, becomeFollowerKE, becomeObserver, becomeWitness, becomeCandidate, becomeLeader, including the check-quorum step-down) calls reset(), which replaces r.readIndex with a new empty instance; contexts registered in the previous instance disappear and no DroppedReadIndexes entry is produced by this path, because droppedReadIndexes is appended only by reportDroppedProposal/reportDroppedReadIndex rejection paths.
knowledge.conditions: A ReadIndex request was registered by the leader, and before its quorum confirmation the node performs any state transition or loses quorum under CheckQuorum.

knowledge.statement: After a node leaves leader state, heartbeat responses cannot confirm a read context: the follower handler map has no HeartbeatResp entry, so defaultHandle performs no action, and onMessageTermNotMatched drops messages whose term is below the local term (sending only a NoOP hint back when the leader-message/CheckQuorum corner case applies).
knowledge.conditions: Leader has stepped down to follower/candidate/observer state, and a HeartbeatResp carrying a read context arrives afterwards with term equal to or lower than the node's term.

knowledge.statement: A ReadIndex request whose SystemCtx was registered but never confirmed or indexed receives no explicit dropped/rejected result from the raft layer and is terminated as RequestTimeout by the node layer: pendingReadIndex.applied and pendingReadIndex.gc mark requests whose deadline has passed, and applied is driven by ordinary event-loop iterations that include LocalTick batches, with the SystemCtx High value bounding batch retention.
knowledge.conditions: The caller supplied a nonzero read-index timeout; the node's event loop continues to process messages (LocalTick included, also when quiesced); no later ready-to-read index for the same context arrives.

knowledge.statement: Outbound raft messages and ReadyToRead entries produced before a state transition in the same Update are still delivered afterwards: reset() replaces readIndex, remotes, observers, witnesses and votes but does not touch r.msgs or r.readyToRead, and Peer.Commit clears them only after the Update has been handed to the node layer (msgs unconditionally, readyToRead when UpdateCommit.ReadyToRead > 0).
knowledge.conditions: A confirmation completes read contexts and produces ReadIndexResp/ReadyToRead, and a state transition (for example the CheckQuorum step-down) occurs later in the same event-loop iteration before the Update is collected and committed.

knowledge.statement: node.doSave classifies state-machine save failures: abort-class errors (ErrSnapshotStopped/ErrSnapshotAborted) remove the temp snapshot directory and report the pending snapshot request as aborted, soft errors (ErrCompacted/ErrSnapshotOutOfDate) return (0, nil) silently, and any other error is returned to the caller; after doSave returns, node.save reports the pending request through pendingSnapshot.apply with ignored set when the returned index is 0.
knowledge.conditions: A snapshot save task (periodic, user-requested or exported) reaches node.save with a non-empty or empty SSRequest key, and rsm.StateMachine.Save returns an error.

knowledge.statement: saveSnapshotRequired only reports a periodic snapshot when SnapshotEntries is non-zero, when both the pushed and applied indexes exceed SnapshotEntries plus the last committed snapshot index and SnapshotEntries plus the last requested snapshot index, and when the state machine is not busy snapshotting; it then records the applied index as the requested index.
knowledge.conditions: A raft update is committed by node.processRaftUpdate after syncing tasks, i.e. the periodic (not user-requested) snapshot trigger.

knowledge.statement: A non-soft error returned by node.save terminates the process from the snapshot worker: ssWorker.save calls panic(err) when node.save returns an error, and neither workerMain nor handle recovers. The only recover in engine.go is installed around step workers when error injection is enabled, and NodeHost.Start's recover wraps only the body of Start and re-panics through panicNow for error values, so a snapshot save error raised later at runtime is not converted into a node-level or cluster-level error.
knowledge.conditions: A snapshot save task is executed by the snapshot worker pool, and node.doSave returns an error other than the abort-class and soft errors it handles internally.

history.statement: A non-soft error returned by node.save terminates the process from the snapshot worker: ssWorker.save calls panic(err) when node.save returns an error, and neither workerMain nor handle recovers. The only recover in engine.go is installed around step workers when error injection is enabled, and nodehost.go's recover wraps NodeHost.Start, so a snapshot save error raised later at runtime is not converted into a node-level or cluster-level error.
history.conditions: A snapshot save task is executed by the snapshot worker pool, and node.doSave returns an error other than the abort-class and soft errors it handles internally.

knowledge.statement: Every non-fatal save outcome completes normally: after node.save returns without error, saveDone records a completed save task through notifySnapshotStatus(save=true) and signals applyReady; the apply worker's processStatusTransition then calls processSaveStatus, which clears the saving flag. This covers the (0, nil) returns for soft errors, abort-class errors (already reported as aborted), and the already-up-to-date early return (reported as rejected through pendingSnapshot.apply).
knowledge.conditions: node.doSave returns without a hard error, including its silent (0, nil) paths; the apply worker keeps running for that cluster.

knowledge.statement: votingMembers() returns a map containing both remotes (full members) and witnesses, so quorum(), broadcastReplicateMessage and broadcastHeartbeatMessageWithHint all treat witnesses as voting participants; hinted heartbeats are therefore sent to witnesses, and a witness answers handleFollowerHeartbeat, which echoes Hint and HintHigh through handleHeartbeatMessage.
knowledge.conditions: Multi-node cluster containing at least one witness; leader sends heartbeats while a read context is registered or during ordinary heartbeat ticks.

knowledge.statement: The captured configuration contract defines a witness as a Raft node without actual log replication and without a state machine, following section 11.7.2 of Ongaro's thesis, and it forbids witness nodes from taking snapshots or being observers. Because raft.votingMembers() includes witnesses, a witness supplies quorum support for elections, commits and read-index confirmation while holding no application data of its own.
knowledge.conditions: A configuration that includes at least one witness; witness support is documented as experimental.

knowledge.statement: A leader replicates to a witness by converting non-config entries into metadata placeholders (config-change entries are sent intact), the witness appends those placeholders and answers with the highest index it received, handleLeaderReplicateResp advances that witness's match through tryUpdate, and tryCommit takes the median of the match values collected from remotes plus witnesses; consequently a two-voter plus witness cluster can commit with the leader's own match and the witness's metadata acknowledgement only. The captured package test TestWitnessReplication asserts this outcome directly: after a proposal in a leader-plus-witness setup it requires the entry to be committed on both the leader and the witness and the witness match to equal the same index.
knowledge.conditions: Cluster contains a witness; leader is broadcasting replicate messages; the witness is reachable and responds while the other voting member does not respond. The recorded test expectation applies to the leader-plus-witness setup built by setUpLeaderAndWitness.

history.statement: A leader replicates to a witness by converting non-config entries into metadata placeholders (config-change entries are sent intact), the witness appends those placeholders and answers with the highest index it received, handleLeaderReplicateResp advances that witness's match through tryUpdate, and tryCommit takes the median of the match values collected from remotes plus witnesses; consequently a two-voter plus witness cluster can commit with the leader's own match and the witness's metadata acknowledgement only.

knowledge.statement: The captured operations documentation defines availability and data loss in terms of quorum membership: a Raft group stays available while it still has quorum, and when the quorum nodes are gone the group cannot be resolved without losing data (with snapshot import offered as the repair path). Combined with the documented witness role, a witness counts as a quorum node that stores no entries, so a configuration can acknowledge commits whose surviving data-bearing copies are fewer than the quorum size.
knowledge.conditions: Documentation statement in the captured tree; applies to any configuration whose quorum includes members without stored entries, such as witness nodes.

knowledge.statement: node.handleProposals drains the incoming proposal queue only when neither the raft rate limiter nor the LogDB busy signal is set: it passes paused into incomingProposals.get, and entryQueue.add rejects new entries while paused, so pausing stops both intake and queue growth. The rate-limiter state used for that decision changes only after ChangeTickThreashold (10) ticks have passed since the last accepted change, with gcTick (3) bounding how long a follower-reported size is considered current.
knowledge.conditions: Proposal path on a node whose InMemRateLimiter is enabled or whose LogDB is reporting busy.

knowledge.statement: The raft in-memory rate limiter's own size is maintained as a live measure of in-memory entries: merge increases it by the appended slice size, sets it to the replacement size when entries replace or truncate earlier ones, sets it to zero on snapshot restore, and appliedLogTo decreases it by exactly the size of the entries that moved below the marker index. The limiter only participates when enabled, so a node with the default disabled limiter never pauses proposals on this account.
knowledge.conditions: InMemRateLimiter enabled for the node; entries appended, replaced, restored from snapshot, or applied by the state machine.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed raft-level harness, a leader of a 3-node test raft that had committed its current-term no-op and registered a ReadIndex context, then lost quorum under a delivered CheckQuorum message, ended in non-leader state with zero entries in droppedReadIndexes and no pending read context in the replacement readIndex instance; a later HeartbeatResp from node 2 carrying that same context added no ReadyToRead entry.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceReadIndexDiscardedOnStepDown in internal/raft with the package in-memory test log; raft layer driven directly without transport, ticks or the node event loop; one schedule.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed object-level harness, a ReadIndex request registered with a five-tick timeout, moved into a read batch under a fresh SystemCtx with no ready-to-read index, then observed after the logical clock reached tick 6 and one applied(0) call, delivered exactly one result on its completed channel with code RequestTimeout.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceReadIndexDeadlineTimeout in the root dragonboat package using a sync.Pool of RequestState, a readIndexQueue of size 16 and a pendingReadIndex; no raft node, nodehost, transport or client invocation; explicit clock advance rather than live ticks.

knowledge.statement: node.requestConfigChange rejects a membership change before any request is created when the node is not initialized, when the node is a witness, or when the change is anything other than node removal and the supplied target fails node.validateTarget; the same validator is applied to every initial member when a cluster is created, and it comes from NodeHostConfig: NodeHostID validation when AddressByNodeHostID is set, the custom transport factory's Validate when one is configured, and address validation otherwise.
knowledge.conditions: Any call path that raises RequestAddNode, RequestAddObserver, RequestAddWitness or RequestDeleteNode, and cluster creation with initial members.

knowledge.statement: inMemory.merge keeps the saved index consistent with truncation: a pure append leaves savedTo unchanged, an append whose first index is at or below the marker replaces the entries and sets savedTo to firstNewIndex-1, and a middle replacement keeps savedTo at min(savedTo, firstNewIndex-1). entriesToSave then returns entries from savedTo+1 onward, so entries removed by a conflicting append are re-reported as not yet saved rather than being treated as already persisted.
knowledge.conditions: A follower appends or replaces raft entries, and the node later commits an Update whose StableLogTo acknowledges persisted entries.

knowledge.statement: A quiesced node runs quiescedTick, which only increments the election tick (and resizes the in-memory log on entry), so leader-specific periodic work does not run: no heartbeat generation, no check-quorum step-down decision, and no pending snapshot acknowledgement timeout. Snapshot status messages themselves still arrive as ordinary messages and are handled through the normal message path.
knowledge.conditions: Cluster quiesce enabled and entered; node ticks while in quiesced state.

knowledge.statement: Every message the node layer processes is recorded in the quiesce state, which resets the idle clock and exits quiesce; a heartbeat or heartbeat response carrying a read context is recorded as read activity rather than being skipped as background traffic. A node therefore enters quiesce only after the idle threshold of electionTick times ten ticks has passed without processed messages, which means any transfer or request that keeps producing acknowledgements keeps the cluster out of quiesce.
knowledge.conditions: Quiesce enabled; messages processed through the node message queue.

knowledge.statement: A RemoveNode config change is accepted even when its target identity is not in the configuration: the address, observer and witness sets are unchanged, the membership's ConfigChangeId advances to the entry index, and the target identity is recorded in the Removed map. A later AddNode for that identity is then rejected because the identity is recorded as removed, so the removal permanently retires an identity that was never a member.
knowledge.conditions: Ordered config changes with a current ConfigChangeId supplied; the removal targets an identity absent from Addresses, Observers and Witnesses; the removal is not the last address of a one-address configuration.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed object-level harness, a pendingProposal created with commit notification enabled delivered RequestCommitted on the committed channel and then RequestCompleted on the completed channel for a fresh proposal, while a proposal registered with a three tick deadline that was ticked to ten and then applied delivered RequestTimeout on the completed channel and no value on the committed channel.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceNotifyCommitContract in the root dragonboat package using a no-op client session, an entryQueue of size eight and a RequestState pool; no raft node, nodehost, transport or state machine.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed object-level harness, a freshly registered session asked about series 1 reported responded=false and update=true; after a response with value 9 was stored, the same question reported responded=false, update=false and returned the stored value 9; after the client acknowledgement advanced to series 1, the same question reported responded=true and update=false.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceSessionExactlyOnce in internal/rsm against a SessionManager with client 42 registered and its responded-to value initially zero; no raft node, state machine or request object.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed object-level harness, an lrusession with capacity two that received clients 11, 22 and 33 in that order, each looked up right after being added and given a stored response, kept clients 22 and 33 with their stored values 22 and 33 and reported client 11 as not kept with no stored value.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceSessionEviction in internal/rsm against newLRUSession(2); only the lrusession object, no state machine or raft node.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed raft-level harness, an entryLog holding indexes 1 to 4 with term 1 reported an empty entriesToSave after an UpdateCommit acknowledged StableLogTo 4, and after tryAppend at LogIndex 2 with term 2 entries at indexes 3 and 4, entriesToSave began at index 3 with length two while the log ended at index 4 with term 2.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceSavedIndexAfterTruncation in internal/raft over the package in-memory test log; no raft node, transport or storage engine.

knowledge.statement: pendingConfigChange holds at most one request: request returns ErrSystemBusy while a request is pending and otherwise stores the generated key with a deadline on its channel; committed(key) delivers the commit-phase result for the matching key without clearing the slot; apply(key, rejected) delivers Completed or Rejected and clears the slot; dropped(key) delivers Dropped and clears it; gc delivers a timeout once the deadline passes and clears it.
knowledge.conditions: A membership change raised through RequestAddNode, RequestAddObserver, RequestAddWitness or RequestDeleteNode with a caller-supplied timeout and commit notification enabled as configured.

knowledge.statement: The snapshot chunk receiver tracks one expected id per snapshot key: a chunk for an unknown key becomes the tracked first chunk only if the slot table is not full, a chunk whose id is not the next expected id is logged and ignored without advancing the expectation, and a chunk whose sender differs from the tracked first chunk's sender is ignored. Only the last chunk triggers validation, finalisation and delivery of the assembled snapshot message, and a saved chunk failure removes the temp directory and terminates through panicNow.
knowledge.conditions: Receiving a chunked snapshot over the transport with the chunk validation option enabled or disabled as configured.

knowledge.statement: Each replica's progress is one of retry, wait, replicate or snapshot. Only retry and replicate are sendable; wait and snapshot report paused so the leader skips them. A non-rejected response advances match through tryUpdate, moves wait to retry and retry to replicate, and moves a snapshot state back to retry once match reaches the snapshot index. A rejected response in retry sets next to match+1 and returns false when the rejection is stale; in other states it also waits for the expected next index, moves to retry and sets next to max(1, min(rejected, last+1)). A completed snapshot status returns the replica to wait with the next index set past the snapshot.
knowledge.conditions: Leader tracking a follower, observer or witness across ordinary replication, rejection, snapshot transfer and idle periods.

knowledge.statement: RequestState.ResultC returns CompletedC directly when commit notification is disabled; otherwise it creates a capacity-two aggregated channel and a goroutine that reads whichever of committedC and CompletedC becomes ready first. If the commit notification is seen, it emits it and then waits for the completion, panicking if the completion is dropped or aborted, is itself a second commit notification, or arrives as committed on the completed channel. If the completion is seen first, it emits it after opportunistically draining a ready commit notification, panicking if a commit notification accompanies a dropped completion. Release returns the state to its pool only after a result has been delivered.
knowledge.conditions: A caller reads ResultC for a proposal or config change that may have commit notification enabled, and releases the state after reading.

knowledge.statement: A proposal is rejected before it reaches the internal queue when its payload exceeds the maximum block size for the configured entry compression, returning ErrPayloadTooBig. Otherwise the request is recorded in the pending map and offered to the entry queue; if the queue is stopped the pending entry is removed and ErrClusterClosed is returned, and if the queue is full the pending entry is removed and ErrSystemBusy is returned, so in both cases no completion is ever delivered for that request.
knowledge.conditions: A client proposal submitted through the node with a caller-supplied timeout and a possibly large or empty command payload.

knowledge.statement: The captured module requires github.com/lni/goutils v1.3.0, which is the module that provides the syncutil package used for the stopper-based worker launch in engine.go; the pin is recorded in go.mod and therefore fixes which implementation of the worker wrapper applies to this snapshot.
knowledge.conditions: Building the captured module with the dependency set recorded in go.mod.

knowledge.statement: The engine's apply loop calls node.handleTask, which delegates to the state machine's Handle, and panics immediately when that call returns an error; the error is not returned to the node, the request layer or the client. A state machine whose Update returns an error therefore terminates the process from the apply worker rather than producing a rejected or failed request result.
knowledge.conditions: A batch of tasks or entries reaches the apply worker after the node's status-transition step, and the state machine's Handle returns a non-nil error.

knowledge.statement: A config change is applied in two stages under the node's raft mutex: the replicated state machine first admits or rejects it in its membership object, then node.ApplyConfigChange forwards the accepted change to the raft peer, which adds or removes the node in its remotes, observers or witnesses and clears the pending-config-change gate; a rejected change skips the peer mutation but still calls RejectConfigChange so the gate is cleared. The node registry is updated in the same call, and a removal of the local node also removes the cluster from the registry and requests local removal.
knowledge.conditions: A committed ConfigChangeEntry is applied by the state machine while the node is running and the change type is one of AddNode, RemoveNode, AddObserver or AddWitness.

knowledge.statement: node.notifyConfigChange computes both role flags from the replicated membership (isObserver from the Observers map, isWitness from the Witnesses map) and stores them in the node's atomic ClusterInfo. node.getClusterInfo rebuilds the value it returns from that record: it copies ClusterID, NodeID, IsObserver, ConfigChangeIndex and Nodes, recomputes IsLeader from the current raft peer and StateMachineType from the local state machine, and never assigns IsWitness; its no-record branch also leaves IsWitness false and sets Pending. Because node.getClusterInfo is the only producer of the elements of NodeHostInfo.ClusterInfoList, the public ClusterInfo.IsWitness returned by NodeHost.GetNodeHostInfo is false for every cluster, including a node whose stored record lists it as a witness.
knowledge.conditions: A node's cluster summary is read through node.getClusterInfo, reached from NodeHost.getClusterInfo and NodeHost.GetNodeHostInfo; the stored record was written by node.notifyConfigChange for a membership that lists the local node in Witnesses, or no record has been stored yet and the Pending branch applies.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed object-level harness, a node whose config.IsWitness is true and whose stored cluster record has IsWitness true reported reported_is_witness=false, reported_is_observer=false, config_index 7, node_count 3 and pending=false; a control node whose stored record instead has IsObserver true reported reported_is_observer=true with config_index 9 and node_count 2; and a witness-configured node with no stored record reported pending=true, config_index 0 and reported_is_witness=false.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceClusterInfoWitnessFlag in the root dragonboat package, calling node.getClusterInfo on nodes that hold a native in-memory state machine and a nil raft peer; the stored ClusterInfo records are supplied directly rather than written by node.notifyConfigChange, and no nodehost, transport, membership or client invocation participates.

knowledge.statement: node.requestLeaderTransfer rejects an uninitialized node and a witness, and otherwise offers the target to a capacity-one channel (NoNode yields an invalid-target error, an occupied channel yields a busy error); node.handleLeaderTransfer consumes that target once per event-loop pass and hands it to Peer.RequestLeaderTransfer, which injects a LeaderTransfer message carrying the target in Hint. Raft dispatches LeaderTransfer only in leader and follower states: a leader requires the target to be one of its remotes and not itself, records it as the transfer target, resets its election tick and sends TimeoutNow immediately when the target is already caught up, while a follower forwards the message once to the leader it knows and drops it with a warning when no leader is known. Candidates, observers and witnesses have no LeaderTransfer handler, and the default handler ignores unknown message types, so a request accepted by those nodes is discarded silently. There is no completion channel on this path; the only caller-visible outcome is the error returned when the request is submitted.
knowledge.conditions: RequestLeaderTransfer or SyncRequestLeaderTransfer is called on any non-witness, initialized node of an existing cluster, including a node that is a follower, candidate or observer at the time the queued target is handed to raft.

knowledge.statement: The raft-layer leadership transfer exists only as leaderTransferTarget and is bounded in time and by authority: handleLeaderTransfer sets it only while the node is leader, reset() calls abortLeaderTransfer so every state transition (including the check-quorum step-down) clears it, leaderTick aborts it once an election timeout has elapsed since the target was set, removing the target node aborts it, and the deferred TimeoutNow for a lagging target is sent only from the replicate-response path guarded by leaderTransfering(), which requires the node to still be leader. While a transfer is in progress the leader drops proposals and reports them as dropped rather than accepting them.
knowledge.conditions: A leader has accepted a leadership-transfer request and is either waiting for the target to catch up, has lost quorum or leadership, or has had the target removed from the configuration.

knowledge.statement: A dropped-proposal notification reaches the client only when raft refuses the proposal message before appending it: the leader refuses while a leadership transfer is in progress, a follower with no known leader drops and reports the proposal, and a candidate drops and reports it. reportDroppedProposal appends the entries to the update's dropped-entry list, and node.processDroppedEntries turns each into a dropped result on the matching pending proposal (or on the pending config change for a config entry). An entry that was appended by a leader and is later overwritten after a leadership change is not on that list, so no dropped result is produced for it; the pending proposal stays registered until its deadline passes, and the pending-proposal tick and gc passes then report the timeout that releases the entry.
knowledge.conditions: A client proposal is accepted by node.requestProposal and reaches raft; the entry is either refused before being appended (transfer in progress, follower without a leader, candidate) or appended and later superseded by another leader's log.

knowledge.statement: While a leader already holds a pending configuration change, a further configuration-change entry in an incoming proposal batch is reported to its client as dropped (reportDroppedConfigChange appends the entry to the dropped-entry list, which the node turns into a dropped result on the pending config change) and the entry itself is replaced by a zero-valued application entry before appendEntries runs; the pending flag is set again in the same loop. The substituted entry carries no type data beyond the application type, so Entry.IsEmpty reports true for it, and the replicated state machine's per-entry dispatch sends it to the noop handler, which only records the applied index and term and reports an empty applied result. A configuration change refused this way therefore leaves a committed log slot that consumes no user command and applies no membership effect.
knowledge.conditions: The leader has a configuration change pending and receives a proposal batch containing at least one further configuration-change entry; the substituted entry is then committed and applied by the replicated state machine.

knowledge.statement: The engine handles each batch of node updates in a fixed order: it collects updates from stepNode, offers the fast-apply subset to the state machine pipeline, sends replicate messages and processes ready-to-read, dropped entries and dropped read indexes, calls logdb.SaveRaftState, handles saved snapshots, then offers the remaining updates to the apply pipeline before appending the entries to the local log and committing the update back to raft. Which pass an update belongs to is decided by setFastApply: the flag starts true, is cleared when the update carries a non-empty snapshot, and is cleared when the last committed entry index falls between the first and last entry being saved in the same update. Consequently an entry written in the current round is never offered to the apply pipeline before that round's log write returns, and the entries offered early are ones an earlier round already persisted.
knowledge.conditions: The engine processes a batch of node updates that may contain both committed entries to apply and entries to save, with or without an installed snapshot.

Which pass an update belongs to is decided by setFastApply: the flag starts true, is cleared when the update carries a non-empty snapshot, and is cleared when the last committed entry index falls between the first and last entry being saved in the same update. Consequently an entry written in the current round is never offered to the apply pipeline before that round's log write returns, and the entries offered early are ones an earlier round already persisted.
history.conditions: The engine processes a batch of node updates that may contain both committed entries to apply and entries to save, with or without an installed snapshot.

knowledge.statement: A snapshot status for a replica that is not in the snapshot progress state is ignored. For a replica in that state with a zero Hint, a rejection clears the pending snapshot index and moves the replica through becomeRetry into the wait state, with next recomputed from the replica's match, while a success moves it to wait with the previous next preserved. Wait is not a sendable state, but the next heartbeat response always calls waitToRetry and, when the replica's match is below the leader's last index, sends it a replicate message, and a non-rejected response that advances match also moves wait to retry. A refused snapshot install therefore returns the replica to ordinary replication on the following heartbeat rather than leaving it stranded or requiring another snapshot.
knowledge.conditions: Leader tracks a follower, observer or witness in the snapshot progress state and receives a snapshot status with a zero hint, rejected or accepted; heartbeats continue to be exchanged.

knowledge.statement: pendingSnapshot holds at most one request: request rejects a zero timeout and a nil channel, returns busy while a request is pending or the snapshot channel will not accept the request, and otherwise queues an rsm.SSRequest carrying its own generated key while storing a request state whose deadline is the current logical tick plus the caller's timeout. The gc pass reports a timeout once the deadline has passed and clears the slot, after which a new request is accepted. apply compares the key of the reported snapshot with the pending state: a matching key yields rejected, aborted or completed (with the snapshot index as the result value) and clears the slot, while a report whose key does not match, including one for a request that already timed out, is ignored without a result. Because the queued snapshot request is not withdrawn when the request state times out, a node can still act on an expired user-requested snapshot.
knowledge.conditions: A user-requested, periodic or exported snapshot request is submitted through the node's pending-snapshot object and is later reported back through apply, or expires through the gc pass, with the logical clock advanced by the node's own ticks.

knowledge.statement: When a snapshot is taken, the replicated state machine builds the snapshot metadata with the applied index and term, the membership, the request, the compression type and a session buffer filled by the session manager's save call, so the client-session table is part of the snapshot stream ahead of the user payload. On recovery the snapshotter opens the snapshot, decompresses it and restores the sessions from that stream before it hands the same stream to the user state machine's recover, so a node that installs or restarts from a snapshot knows which client series it has already answered. The witness snapshot is the deliberate exception: it is written with an empty session table because a witness holds no state machine and no client sessions.
knowledge.conditions: A snapshot is saved by a non-witness node and later restored by the same node at restart or installed on a follower; the session manager is the one belonging to the node's replicated state machine.

knowledge.statement: The captured client contract makes series advancement a caller duty tied to success: the asynchronous proposal documentation states that on a timeout the caller may retry the same proposal without updating the session, that a rejection usually means the session was evicted and the client should be treated as failed, and that only a successful completion requires calling ProposalCompleted; the synchronous entry point states the same rule in terms of its timeout and invalid-session errors, and the captured Chinese overview says that a timed-out proposal is retried directly without calling ProposalCompleted. The session helper enforces the discipline: ProposalCompleted advances the series and the acknowledged value only when the current series id is exactly one ahead of the acknowledged value and otherwise panics, and the validity check used before proposing rejects a session whose acknowledged value has overtaken its series. A client that follows the contract therefore retries a timed-out proposal under the same series, which is the input the server's session decisions need in order to return the stored result instead of applying the command again.
knowledge.conditions: A client uses a regular (non-NO-OP) session to propose to a state machine that supports session-managed updates, and the proposal ends with a timeout, a rejection, or a successful completion.

knowledge.statement: In the fixed object-level harness, a native state machine that consumed an AddNode entry for node 1 followed by an AddWitness entry for node 2 ended with one member address, one witness and the local node listed as a witness at configuration-change index 2; node.notifyConfigChange then stored a cluster record with the witness flag true, the observer flag false, configuration index 2 and one member, while node.getClusterInfo reported the witness flag false with the pending flag false and the same configuration index and member count.
knowledge.conditions: Single execution of TestAssuranceWitnessRecordFromMembership in the root dragonboat package; the configuration-change entries are marshalled into entry payloads and delivered as one task through the state machine's own task queue, the node has a system-event listener with no user listener and a dummy node proxy, and no raft peer, transport or nodehost participates.

knowledge.statement: Committed entries reach the state machine through a task pushed with the entries to apply and the pushed index set to the last entry of that batch; when the raft update for a cluster reports that more committed entries remain, the engine re-arms that cluster's step worker, so the next step iteration collects the following batch of committed entries rather than waiting for new raft activity. The apply path therefore drains a backlog over successive iterations instead of stalling on a consumed batch.
knowledge.conditions: A cluster has more committed entries than the batch handed to the apply path in one iteration, and the update built for that cluster reports that more committed entries remain.

knowledge.statement: A linearizable read registers a read request with the node and marks the cluster ready to step, then waits on that request state before invoking the user state machine's lookup on the same node. The request state is completed by the node's applied-index pass, which completes only batches that carry a ready-to-read index and whose index has been reached by the applied index; a registered batch whose index is still zero is not completed by that pass. Consequently the lookup that produces the answer runs against state that already includes every entry up to the index the ReadIndex protocol confirmed, rather than against local state from before that confirmation.
knowledge.conditions: A client issues a linearizable read through the node host with a deadline, the node registers the read and the ReadIndex protocol later produces a ready-to-read index for it, and the node's state machine keeps applying entries.

interpretations.rationale: Current conclusion: a ReadIndex request outstanding when the leader loses authority keeps a legal, bounded terminal path, and a deposed leader cannot complete it from stale confirmations, although the terminal result is RequestTimeout rather than an explicit dropped result. Basis: (1) the leader only registers a read context after it has a committed entry at its current term (internal/raft/raft.go:1662-1696), otherwise it reports the context in droppedReadIndexes and node.processDroppedReadIndexes forwards that to pendingReadIndex.dropped (node.go:1021-1026); (2) registration is followed immediately by heartbeats carrying that context, and confirmation needs quorum-1 matching responses plus the leader's implicit count, at which point earlier contexts are released with the later index and either a local ReadyToRead is added or a ReadIndexResp is sent (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:30-116); (3) every state transition, including the CheckQuorum step-down at raft.go:1608-1615, runs reset() which installs a fresh readIndex (raft.go:1003-1025), so registered contexts are discarded without any DroppedReadIndexes entry; (4) after the step-down the node cannot confirm them from heartbeat responses, because follower state has no HeartbeatResp handler (raft.go:2116-2129) and lower-term messages are dropped (raft.go:1430-1478), and Peer.Handle additionally ignores responses from unknown peers (peer.go:185-196); (5) consequently the node-layer batch keeps index 0 and is terminated by pendingReadIndex.applied/gc as RequestTimeout once the caller-supplied deadline passes, which is reached from ordinary event-loop iterations because LocalTick messages make handleEvents report an event and call pendingReadIndexes.applied (node.go:1132-1166, 1478-1492; request.go:908-954, 403-414). Counterevidence considered: handleCandidateReadIndex reports the same context twice (raft.go:1998-2012 plus reportDroppedReadIndex), but pendingReadIndex.dropped deletes the batch on the first delivery, so the duplicate result is a no-op rather than a double notification; and handleFollowerReadIndexResp does set the leader id and add a ready-to-read, but only for a context the leader confirmed before the transition, so it does not resurrect authority for a discarded context. Limitations: this account is source-only for this revision and rests on the node event loop being driven while the request is pending; it does not measure how long the timeout path takes, does not claim the timeout code is the most useful client-visible result, and does not cover the same-batch confirmation/reset race named in the registered gap.

1b1f6ec36e5540a5a256dc25dd86cc61-gap-0.explanation: The window does not exist as stated. handleLeaderHeartbeatResp calls handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation, which calls readIndex.confirm and then immediately appends either ReadyToRead (r.addReadyToRead) or a ReadIndexResp message (r.send) for every completed status; no state transition or reset can intervene inside that call frame, and confirmation is a prerequisite for those emissions. A step-down later in the same event-loop iteration does not discard them: reset() rebuilds readIndex/remotes/observers/witnesses/votes but leaves r.msgs and r.readyToRead untouched (raft.go:1003-1025), and they are cleared only by Peer.Commit after the Update carrying them has been handed to the node layer (peer.go:284-294; readyToRead only when UpdateCommit.ReadyToRead > 0). The deadline path established earlier therefore remains a fallback for contexts that were never confirmed, not for a confirmed context whose response was lost in the same batch.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: no defect is established yet; the question is whether a hard snapshot-save error can strand the periodic snapshot duty. What the sources do establish: saveSnapshotRequired advances the requested index (ss.setReqIndex(applied)) before any save runs and suppresses new periodic requests while the state machine reports busy snapshotting (node.go:651-667); doSave already holds the save state when it calls n.sm.Save and, on a hard error, returns the error to node.save without itself reporting a terminal snapshot result (node.go:693-760); node.save reports the pending user/periodic request only after doSave returns a value, so a hard error bypasses that report (node.go:693-706; request.go:648-668). What remains undecided is the enclosing control flow: whether the save task error propagates to rsm.StateMachine.Handle and the node worker in a way that clears the saving flag through processSaveStatus (node.go:1451-1467) or terminates the node, and whether n.ss.reqSnapshotIndex is ever reset after such a failure. Until that control flow is traced, the possible outcomes are a one-off failed snapshot request (no defect) or a durable suppression of snapshots and therefore of automatic log compaction (bounded progress defect), and the account stays unresolved.

knowledge.assertion: Hard save errors are returned to the caller of node.save, while abort-class and soft errors are handled inside doSave.
The periodic snapshot trigger depends on SnapshotEntries, the snapshot index, the requested index and the busy-snapshotting check.

counterevidence: processSaveStatus exists and clears the saving flag when a completed save task is available, which would make a failure recoverable if the failed task is still delivered through the completion path.
limitations: Source reading only for this revision; the error propagation from rsm.StateMachine.Handle to the node worker has not been traced yet.
No execution evidence; a harness would need a state machine whose Save fails once and then succeeds to observe whether a later periodic snapshot is still requested.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the suspicion is refuted within the traced scope. A periodic snapshot save that fails with a hard error does not leave a live node whose snapshot duty is silently suppressed, and the non-fatal outcomes do not either. Basis: (1) saveSnapshotRequired advances ss.reqSnapshotIndex only when it actually requests a snapshot and suppresses further periodic requests while n.isBusySnapshotting() reports busy (node.go:651-667); (2) the save task is executed by ssWorker.save, which calls panic(err) on any error from node.save and has no recover in workerMain or handle (engine.go:275-305); the recover at engine.go:1029-1044 is installed only for step workers when error injection is enabled, and nodehost.go's recover covers NodeHost.Start, so a runtime save error ends the process instead of leaving the save flag set with a node that keeps applying entries; (3) on every non-fatal path, node.save returns nil and node.saveDone stores a completed save task via notifySnapshotStatus(save=true) and signals applyReady (node.go:846-850; snapshotstate.go:185-211), and the apply worker calls processStatusTransition before handleTask, so processSaveStatus clears the saving flag and later periodic snapshots remain enabled (engine.go:1200-1212; node.go:1451-1467); (4) the (0, nil) paths inside doSave are the soft-error case, the abort case that already reported aborted through pendingSnapshot.apply, and the already-up-to-date early return, in which node.save reports the pending user request as rejected (node.go:693-760; request.go:648-668). Counterevidence considered: a hard error bypasses the pendingSnapshot report for that request, but since the process panics at the same point, no client-visible state is retained in a live node, so it cannot strand later snapshot requests. Limitations: this is a source argument, not an execution; it does not cover a state machine whose Save blocks indefinitely (no error at all), nor storage faults inside snapshotter.commit that return errors handled elsewhere, nor whether process termination is an acceptable recovery policy versus returning an error to the caller. The claim is limited to the periodic-save control flow in this snapshot.

9bf8b80283c042d1b383e211c89c1701-gap-1.explanation: No such state survives. A non-soft error makes node.save return an error, and ssWorker.save panics on that error with no recover around workerMain/handle (engine.go:275-305; the engine recover at 1029-1044 is restricted to step workers under error injection and nodehost.go's recover wraps only NodeHost.Start), so the node does not continue with the saving flag set or an advanced requested index. On the non-fatal paths the flag is cleared: node.save returns nil, saveDone records a completed save task (node.go:846-850; snapshotstate.go:185-211), and the apply worker's processStatusTransition/processSaveStatus clears saving before executing the next task (engine.go:1200-1212; node.go:1451-1467). n.ss.reqSnapshotIndex does not need an explicit reset for recovery because saveSnapshotRequired compares applied against SnapshotEntries plus the requested index, so the next request occurs once applied advances by a further SnapshotEntries window; only restart resets it, and restart also resets the process that would have carried a stale session. The gap is resolved as a refutation of the stranding hypothesis.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the eligibility behavior is established but the correctness judgment is not. votingMembers() merges remotes and witnesses (raft.go:418-428), so quorum() counts witnesses and broadcastHeartbeatMessageWithHint sends the read context to every voting member including witnesses (raft.go:839-852). A witness handles a leader heartbeat through handleWitnessHeartbeat -> handleFollowerHeartbeat -> handleHeartbeatMessage, which echoes Hint and HintHigh in the response (raft.go:1316-1325), and Peer.Handle admits responses from known witnesses (peer.go:185-196), so handleLeaderHeartbeatResp can pass that response to handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation, where readIndex.confirm counts it toward quorum-1 without checking whether the responder is a witness (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). What is not decided is correctness: a witness is a voting member that votes in elections and stores metadata entries only, so its confirmation that it has not granted a higher-term vote may be exactly the evidence the read protocol needs, in which case the behavior is intended and safe; the alternative reading is that a data-bearing majority is also required for reads. The question stays open with no defect claim, and the gap records the concrete configuration (for example voters {A,B} plus witness W with quorum 2, where A is leader and only W responds) that would settle it.

counterevidence: handleLeaderReadIndex explicitly refuses to serve a ReadIndex request whose requester is a witness (raft.go:1662-1676), showing the author distinguished witness requesters from witness voters; that asymmetry is consistent with counting witness confirmations deliberately.
limitations: Source reading only; no execution and no documentary statement of witness duties has been located in the captured tree yet.
Does not establish whether a witness-only confirmation can coexist with an unreachable data-bearing majority, which is the configuration that would matter for read availability.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: counting a witness's heartbeat response toward a leader's ReadIndex confirmation is consistent with the captured witness contract, so the eligibility behavior is not a defect. Basis: (1) the configuration contract states that a witness is a Raft node without actual log replication and without a state machine, citing section 11.7.2 of Ongaro's thesis, and it disallows witness snapshots and the observer role (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220); in that thesis section witnesses are voting members used to keep quorum without storing data. (2) raft.votingMembers() merges remotes and witnesses, so quorum() counts witnesses and broadcastHeartbeatMessageWithHint delivers the read context to them (raft.go:418-428, 839-852); a witness echoes Hint/HintHigh through handleHeartbeatMessage (raft.go:1316-1325), Peer.Handle admits its response (peer.go:185-196), and readIndex.confirm counts accepted responders toward quorum-1 (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). (3) The ReadIndex protocol's confirmation step asks whether the leader still holds authority at its term; a witness that answers with the current term has not granted a vote to a higher-term candidate, which is the evidence the step needs, and it needs no stored entries because the returned index is the leader's commit index and the requester completes only after its own applied index reaches it. (4) The asymmetry at handleLeaderReadIndex, which refuses witness requesters (raft.go:1662-1676), is consistent with this reading: witnesses confirm leadership but do not serve reads. Counterevidence considered: a configuration of voters {A,B} plus witness W with quorum 2 can complete a read confirmation with A and W while B is unreachable, so witness support is load-bearing for read availability; that follows from the documented voter role rather than from an accidental counting path. Limitations: this rests on the documented contract plus source reasoning, not on an execution or on a documented statement about read-index specifically; it does not claim that a witness-only confirmation preserves data availability in the sense of committed-entry durability, which the witness design trades away by not storing entries; and it does not settle whether the experimental witness feature should be strengthened beyond the thesis role.

37b5dc8bae1c4a87883de59ff9d8463f-gap-2.explanation: Yes, a read context can complete with a witness confirmation and no other non-leader full member, for example with voters {A,B} plus witness W where quorum is 2, A leads and only W echoes the context. That support is sufficient for the read protocol's purpose because the confirmation only establishes that no higher-term vote has been granted within a quorum of the current configuration, and the witness is a documented voting member that holds no log (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220; raft.go:418-428, 839-852, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). The requester still waits for its own applied index to reach the confirmed commit index, so the witness is never asked to supply entries. The eligibility is therefore by design rather than an unintended counting path; the durability trade-off (a quorum can be assembled without a second data-bearing copy) is a property of the documented witness role and responsibility of the deployment, not a defect in the confirmation code.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the commit-support behavior is established, the correctness judgment is not. makeReplicateMessage replaces non-config entries with metadata placeholders when the target is a witness (raft.go:718-750), the witness appends them and answers with LogIndex equal to the last index in the message through handleReplicateMessage, and the leader advances that witness's match in handleLeaderReplicateResp via rp.tryUpdate (raft.go:1697-1727). tryCommit builds its matched array from remotes and witnesses, so with two voters and one witness the sorted array has three values and the median is reached by the leader plus the witness alone (raft.go:418-428, 891-912). The configuration contract describes a witness as a voter without log replication or a state machine and forbids it snapshots (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220), so no member ever asks the witness for data; the consequence is that such a cluster can acknowledge a committed entry whose only data-bearing copy is the leader. Whether that is a defect or a documented deployment trade-off is what remains open: the witness role explicitly excludes stored data, which suggests the durability limit is intrinsic to the role rather than a bug in tryCommit, but the captured tree has not yet been shown to state failure tolerance for witness configurations, so the account stays unresolved with no defect claim.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a commit that rests on the leader plus a witness is a documented consequence of quorum membership, not an implementation defect. Basis: (1) a leader sends a witness metadata placeholders in place of non-config entries (raft.go:718-750), the witness acknowledges the last index it received through handleReplicateMessage, and the leader advances that witness's match in handleLeaderReplicateResp (raft.go:1697-1727); (2) tryCommit builds its matched array from remotes plus witnesses and takes the median, so with two voters and one witness the leader's own match plus the witness acknowledgement reaches the commit index (raft.go:418-428, 891-912); (3) the configuration contract defines a witness as a voter without log replication or a state machine (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220), and the captured operations documentation states that the group is available while it has quorum and that losing the quorum nodes means losing data, with snapshot import as the documented repair path (docs/devops.md:9-11). Read together, the quorum a client relies on may contain a member that stores nothing, so the resulting durability limit belongs to the declared configuration semantics; no commit-time check promises a data-bearing acknowledgement. Counterevidence considered: the behavior does make witness availability load-bearing for commit progress and reduces the number of data copies behind a successful acknowledgement; that is a deployment trade-off visible from the documented contract, and the tree offers no statement that witnesses change the quorum rule or that commits require a data-storing supporter. Limitations: this rests on documentation plus source reasoning, with no execution; it does not validate that operators actually read the trade-off, and it does not cover configurations mixing observers or multiple witnesses beyond what votingMembers shows. The claim is limited to the witness commit path and does not assert general durability guarantees for non-witness clusters.

38116b05f0304877af38e351c44578a1-gap-3.explanation: The captured tree states the general quorum rule rather than a witness-specific one: docs/devops.md says the Raft group is available while it still has quorum and that when the quorum nodes are gone the data cannot be resolved without loss, pointing at snapshot import as the repair path, and config/config.go defines a witness as a voter with no log replication and no state machine. There is no statement requiring commit support from a member that stores the entry, and no commit-time check enforcing one: tryCommit uses the median match over remotes plus witnesses only. The consequence is therefore bounded by the documented quorum contract, which the witness role changes in kind (a quorum node without stored entries) rather than in rule.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the pause mechanism is established; whether it can hold indefinitely is not. handleProposals computes paused from the raft rate limiter and the LogDB busy signal and passes it to incomingProposals.get, and entryQueue.add refuses new entries while paused, so a paused node stops both draining and growing the queue (node.go:1206-1223; queue.go add). InMemRateLimiter.RateLimited accepts a new measurement only when at least ChangeTickThreashold ticks have elapsed since the last accepted change, and limitedByInMemSize ignores follower sizes older than gcTick and compares against 70% of the maximum while already limited (internal/server/rate.go:20-30, 155-193), so the gate has deliberate hysteresis. The partial evidence that the gate releases is that applying entries shrinks the in-memory log and is expected to Decrease the recorded size (internal/raft/inmemory.go:143-165), and application progress depends on committed entries reaching the state machine rather than on new proposals. What is not yet established is whether the applied-index path is the only driver of size reduction for the component that triggers the limit, whether follower-reported sizes can hold it up, and whether the LogDB busy signal has an independent release path. Until those are traced the account stays unresolved with no defect claim; the registered gap states the concrete next check.

knowledge.assertion: Proposal intake is paused by the rate limiter or LogDB busy signal, and the rate limiter applies hysteresis before changing state.

counterevidence: The limiter's hysteresis exists to avoid flapping and is paired with a follower-state gc window, so the sticky state may be intentional rather than a stall.
limitations: Source reading only; the applied-index size accounting and the LogDB busy signal's release path have not been traced yet.
Does not quantify how long a paused node stays paused under a steady high-size workload.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the proposal pause is not self-sustaining within the traced scope, so the suspicion of an unbounded intake stall is refuted. Basis: (1) the limiter's own size is a live measure, not a monotone counter: merge increases it by the appended slice size (internal/raft/inmemory.go:205-206), replaces it with the resulting size when entries replace or truncate earlier ones (215, 226), clears it on snapshot restore (241), and appliedLogTo decreases it by the size of exactly the entries moved below the marker (162); (2) entries leave the in-memory region when the state-machine worker applies committed entries, which is driven by committed log content and application progress rather than by admitting new proposals, so pausing intake cannot keep the measure from falling; (3) the other components consulted by limitedByInMemSize are follower-reported sizes, which are ignored and garbage-collected once older than gcTick ticks (internal/server/rate.go:168-204), and the limiter accepts a state change after at most the hysteresis window of ChangeTickThreashold ticks (155-166); (4) handleProposals recomputes paused on every event-loop iteration, so once the measure drops below the threshold the queue is drained again (node.go:1206-1223). Counterevidence considered: a node whose committed-but-unapplied backlog genuinely exceeds the configured in-memory limit will keep proposals paused for as long as application lags, which is the intended backpressure and could look like a stall under a badly sized limit or a slow state machine; that is a configuration and workload property, and the release still depends on application progress rather than on intake. Limitations: source reasoning only, no execution; the claim does not cover a state machine that stops applying entirely, a LogDB busy signal whose worker never completes (storage faults are fatal elsewhere), or whether the hysteresis latency is acceptable for a given workload.

b1532231bc7a45cb88f4c1cbac908f9c-gap-4.explanation: Yes. appliedLogTo decreases the recorded size by exactly the applied slice size for every entry that moves below the in-memory marker (internal/raft/inmemory.go:138-165), and merge maintains the same measure on append, replacement and restore (199-241). Applying entries requires no new proposals: the apply path consumes committed entries handed to the state machine and signals readiness independently, and handleProposals recomputes the paused decision on each event-loop iteration. Follower-reported sizes, the other input to limitedByInMemSize, are discarded after gcTick ticks. So a rate-limited node returns to accepting proposals once the committed backlog is applied and the measure falls below the release threshold, provided the limiter is enabled at all and the state machine keeps applying.

knowledge.assertion: Proposal intake is paused by the rate limiter or LogDB busy signal, and the rate limiter applies hysteresis before changing state.
The in-memory size measure is maintained by merge, restore and appliedLogTo, and falls when entries are applied.

counterevidence: A genuinely large committed backlog keeps the pause in place until application catches up, so the pause length follows application throughput rather than a fixed bound.
The limiter's hysteresis delays the release by up to ChangeTickThreashold ticks after the measure falls below the threshold.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the mechanism is partly traced; whether a stalled snapshot resumes without external activity is not established. A quiesced node's tick path calls quiescedTick, which increments the election tick and resizes the in-memory log on entry but does not run leaderTick (raft.go:632-638; node.go:1478-1492). leaderTick is where heartbeats are generated, where check quorum is raised, and where checkPendingSnapshotAck is called to force a snapshot status decision when acknowledgements stop (raft.go:600-631, 1832-1861). SnapshotStatus messages are ordinary messages, so acknowledgements that do arrive are still processed and can clear the remote's snapshot state; the open question is the case where acknowledgements stop, because the timeout that would move the remote out of snapshot state is tick-driven. The candidate outcomes are: the transfer resumes when any cluster activity exits quiesce and leaderTick runs (bounded by activity, so a deployment property rather than a defect), or some independent retry path exists and no stall is possible. Until that is traced, the account stays unresolved with no defect claim.

counterevidence: Quiesce is an opt-in bandwidth optimisation, so a transfer that waits for the next activity may be an accepted consequence rather than a defect.
limitations: Source reading only; neither the follower-side snapshot retry path nor transport reconnect behaviour has been traced.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: an in-flight snapshot cannot be stranded indefinitely by quiesce alone, because the transfer's own acknowledgements keep the leader out of quiesce and any later message restarts the tick-driven backstop. Basis: (1) each processed message is recorded in the quiesce state, which resets the idle clock and exits quiesce, and hinted heartbeats are recorded as read activity rather than ignored (node.go:1266-1272); (2) entry into quiesce requires an idle interval of electionTick times ten ticks (quiesce.go:81-99), so a stream that keeps producing acknowledgements keeps the node active and leaderTick keeps calling checkPendingSnapshotAck (raft.go:600-631, 1832-1861); (3) a stalled transfer is precisely the case in which acknowledgements stop, so the cluster may fall into quiesce and the ack timeout is suspended while quiesced (raft.go:632-638; node.go:1478-1492); (4) the suspension ends as soon as any message is processed, because that both exits quiesce and gives leaderTick a chance to run, at which point the pending ack timer resumes counting and can drive the remote out of snapshot state. Counterevidence considered: if the cluster receives no further messages at all, the transfer stays pending indefinitely, but that condition also means there is no client activity, no replication traffic and no follower progress to protect; it is a quiescent-cluster property rather than a hidden loss of the transfer's completion, because the transfer re-arms when the cluster wakes. Limitations: this is a source argument, not an execution; it does not cover a follower that remains reachable but silently drops acknowledgements while also sending nothing else, nor does it bound the time to resume after waking, which depends on the next tick.

472e9ca7e8a8446391293cd2f1b50f23-gap-6.explanation: The independent driver is the stream's own traffic and, after a stall, the next message that wakes the node. Acknowledgements are ordinary received messages, they are recorded into the quiesce state, and that recording resets the idle clock and exits quiesce (node.go:1266-1272; quiesce.go:81-99). While the cluster stays awake, leaderTick runs and checkPendingSnapshotAck can force a snapshot status decision when acks stop. If acks stop and the cluster then quiesces, no component retries by itself; the transfer re-arms on the next processed message, which restarts leaderTick. The stall is therefore bounded by cluster activity rather than by an internal timer during quiesce.

knowledge.assertion: Quiesced ticks skip leaderTick, so heartbeat, check-quorum and snapshot-ack timeout work does not run while quiesced.
Every processed message resets the idle clock and exits quiesce, so transfer traffic keeps the leader ticking.

counterevidence: With no messages at all the transfer remains pending; the justification for calling that acceptable is that the cluster is idle, not that the transfer is guaranteed to finish.
limitations: Source reasoning only; no execution of a stalled stream under quiesce.
Does not cover a follower that drops acknowledgements yet sends nothing else, nor the resume latency after waking.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a proposal whose entry was appended and then superseded after a leadership change ends with the caller's deadline outcome rather than a dropped notification, and the node layer keeps no orphaned bookkeeping for it. The notifying paths are narrow and enumerated: raft refuses a proposal message while a leadership transfer is in progress (raft.go:1615-1625), on a follower with no known leader (raft.go:1905-1912) and on a candidate (raft.go:1993-1997); each calls reportDroppedProposal, which appends the entries to r.droppedEntries (raft.go:2052-2061), Peer.update copies them into the update's dropped-entry list (peer.go:352-355), and node.processDroppedEntries converts each into pendingProposals.dropped or pendingConfigChange.dropped through the entry key (node.go:1027-1036; request.go:1015-1020). A leader that accepted entries has already handed them to raft; if a later leader overwrites those indexes, raft has no message of its own to report, and no other path adds the entry to the dropped list, so the client's request state is not completed by a drop. It is still completed: the proposal shard's tick marks the request expired once the caller deadline passes and its gc delivers RequestTimeout and clears the pending entry (request.go:1031-1045), which is the same terminal path recorded for an expired proposal with commit notification enabled. Two consequences bound the account rather than undermine it. Config changes share the notifying path: a refused config-change entry is reported through pendingConfigChange.dropped, so the membership request does not wait for its deadline on those paths.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the entry that replaces a refused configuration change is inert, and the requesting client still gets a dropped result, so the substitution does not smuggle an empty command into the user state machine. The refusal happens in the leader's proposal handler: for each configuration-change entry, if a change is already pending the handler reports it through reportDroppedConfigChange and overwrites that slice element with a zero-valued application entry, then sets the pending flag and appends the batch (raft.go:1616-1636; reportDroppedConfigChange at raft.go:2048-2050 appends the original entry to the dropped-entry list). The node layer consumes that list in processDroppedEntries, which routes a configuration-change entry to pendingConfigChange.dropped and thereby delivers Dropped and clears the request slot (node.go:1027-1036), so the caller is not left waiting for its deadline. The substituted entry is not a command: Entry.IsEmpty reports true for an entry that is neither a configuration change nor session managed and whose payload is absent (raftpb/raft.go:157-175), and the state machine's dispatch for a non-configuration, non-session-managed entry takes the empty branch, calls the noop handler and reports an empty applied result, panicking only on the impossible case of a non-empty, non-session-managed entry (statemachine.go:878-895). The noop handler's only effects are recording the applied index and term (statemachine.go:993-1000), so the committed slot advances application progress without invoking the user's Update or exposing an empty command. Two consequences worth stating: the cluster's log gains one extra no-op entry per refused configuration change, which is accounted for in the applied index and therefore in the compaction thresholds, and a badly behaved batch that mixed a dropped change with valid proposals would still append the valid entries, since only the configuration-change element is replaced.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the engine has no path that offers an entry to the state machine before that entry is durably written on the local node, and the early apply pass is limited to entries persisted in an earlier round. The ordering is explicit in the step loop: node.stepNode gathers updates, applySnapshotAndUpdate with fastApply=true processes only updates marked FastApply, replicate messages and the ready-to-read, dropped-entry and dropped-read-index handling follow, then logdb.SaveRaftState runs, then applySnapshotAndUpdate with fastApply=false processes the remaining updates and each node appends its entries to the local log and hands the commit back to raft (engine.go:1290-1338, 1354-1375). The selector that decides membership in the early pass is setFastApply: the flag starts true, a non-empty snapshot clears it, and a committed-entries tail that falls inside the saved range clears it (peer.go:199-226). So an entry that is being written in this round can only be applied in the second pass, after the write returned; an entry applied in the first pass was already written by an earlier round, and node.processRaftUpdate appends exactly the entries that still need writing before the update is committed back to raft (node.go:1077-1096). Durability of a completed client request therefore does not rest on this ordering alone: an entry is applied only once it is committed, and commit requires that a quorum of voting members stored it, so a completed proposal is recoverable from a surviving quorum even if the responding node crashes after replying. Two bounds worth keeping with the account: the apply pipeline is asynchronous, so the ordering above constrains when entries are offered to the state machine rather than when the user's Update returns, and the fast-apply optimisation does let a node apply entries whose local write happened in an earlier round while a later round is still writing, which is consistent with quorum durability but means local log state can trail the applied index during that window.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a rejected snapshot install cannot strand a replica, because the leader returns it to ordinary replication on the next heartbeat. The reject path is explicit: the snapshot status handler ignores messages from replicas that are not in the snapshot state, and for a status with a zero hint it clears the pending snapshot index, then calls becomeWait for both the accepted and rejected cases (raft.go:1792-1810). becomeWait clears the snapshot acknowledgement, calls becomeRetry - which, for a replica still in the snapshot state, sets next to the larger of match+1 and snapshotIndex+1, and the snapshot index has just been cleared, so next becomes match+1 - and then moves the state to wait (remote.go:104-129). Wait is a paused state, so the leader sends no replication while it lasts, but the state is not terminal: the heartbeat response handler calls waitToRetry unconditionally and then sends a replicate message whenever the replica's match is below the leader's last index (raft.go:1728-1740), and tryUpdate itself calls waitToRetry whenever an accepted response advances match (remote.go:143-156). Because heartbeats are sent on the leader's heartbeat tick to every voting member and to observers, the window in which the replica is paused is bounded by the next heartbeat response, after which it is retried from match+1 and can receive either entries or, if the gap is beyond the log, another snapshot. Two bounds belong with this account: the recovery assumes the follower keeps answering heartbeats, and the wait window is therefore measured in heartbeats rather than in a count of ticks the leader can guarantee; and if the leader is quiesced, the earlier recorded quiesce behaviour applies, since any processed message exits quiesce and restarts the tick-driven work.

counterevidence: A rejection does not immediately resume replication: while the replica sits in the wait state it is paused, so repair waits at least until the next heartbeat response rather than happening within the same handling of the status message.
